title: Leya Rebrands as Legora: Collaborative AI for Lawyers
author: Chris Williams · Zach Abramowitz

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Conditional optimism: User problems outrank AI branding
st.an: The source documents Legora’s rapid headcount growth, broad recruitment and office expansion, illustrating company-level opportunities across legal, technical and commercial roles. It does not address whether legal AI adoption should be user-problem-led, distinguish assistance from autonomy, or provide evidence of AI performance and transformation, so its position on the cluster’s principal proposition cannot be determined.
qs: So whether that's in like your kind of go to market, business development, whether that is in your kind of account management, legal engineering, software engineering, all those roles, we are hiring across the board at the moment.
I think in March last year, the team was about eight people, and we had our town hall a couple of weeks ago, and there were 70 of us on the call.

st.t: Expertise pipeline: Automated work weakens succession routes
st.an: Legora anticipates significant but uncertain changes in legal practice and promotes collaboration between lawyers and technical experts. However, it does not address whether automation weakens apprenticeship, associate leverage or partner succession, nor does it propose explicit funding, simulation, feedback or broader career paths for preserving the expertise pipeline.
qs: You bring the domain expertise, we bring the technical expertise, and we collaborate.
No one can truly say in one year this is where AI is going to be.

st.t: Legal workflows: Contextual agents remain lawyer-guided
st.an: The source treats easier generative-AI sales as an early signal of fundamental change in legal work, but offers only anecdotal enthusiasm and product endorsement. It does not address the cluster’s central claims about workflow redesign, legal context, integration, lawyer guidance or verification, so its position on those propositions cannot be determined.
qs: Like I was selling a product that was really hard to sell, even if I knew that it would provide value to the customers versus now selling generative AI to legal, which was a different world.
Yeah, so I mean, I obviously with the rise of tools like ChatGPT, right, I saw that there was a technology on the horizon that could really make fundamental changes to the way that people operate.

st.t: Vendor strategy: Faster building cannot eliminate integration
st.an: The source indicates that generative AI is changing legal-tech sales and may fundamentally alter legal work, which loosely aligns with the cluster’s broader account of strategic change. However, it provides no evidence on faster software development, build-versus-buy decisions, workflow integration, migration or adoption constraints, so its position on the cluster’s principal proposition cannot be determined.
qs: Like I was selling a product that was really hard to sell, even if I knew that it would provide value to the customers versus now selling generative AI to legal, which was a different world.
Yeah, so I mean, I obviously with the rise of tools like ChatGPT, right, I saw that there was a technology on the horizon that could really make fundamental changes to the way that people operate.

st.t: Agentic delegation: Multistep work moves verification bottlenecks
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s central proposition that agentic AI executes connected workflows but should not presently operate without meaningful lawyer review. It reinforces the cluster’s distinction between multistep execution and unchecked autonomy, while offering product claims and forecasts rather than measured evidence of reliability or savings.
qs: You can have an agent that can then be basically given a plan to this is the workflow, these are the steps.
And frankly, the quality of AI is not really at the point where you're going to just trust an agent to go and do that work for you and just blindly send it to a client, right?

st.t: Agentic workflows: Tacit expertise resists easy transfer
st.an: The source aligns with the cluster’s core proposition by presenting agentic legal AI as a structured, multistep workflow adaptable to firms and teams, while insisting that lawyers review and control outputs rather than rely on autonomous delivery. Its architecture and performance claims are vendor-reported and do not independently establish reliability or resolve the transfer of tacit expertise.
qs: Rather, we've built an agent that has different steps, a different process that it goes through to articulate the questions that has been given, and then to kind of apply that to legal thinking, as opposed to trying to fine tune the models to have ChatGPT that understands law.
And frankly, the quality of AI is not really at the point where you're going to just trust an agent to go and do that work for you and just blindly send it to a client, right?

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s diagnosis that AI will reduce routine junior production, shrink the junior layer and shift lawyers earlier toward reviewing outputs and exercising judgment. It also acknowledges uncertainty about what replaces displaced work. However, its claims are predictive and anecdotal, and it does not address how juniors will acquire the expertise needed for verification or propose deliberate training mechanisms.
qs: And if you look at them all at equal portions, you see that that kind of real junior layer is shrinking.

So you people are having to step up quicker into a role, where they're not the ones that are doing the hard, mundane, heavy lifting, but actually more take our legal knowledge and be able to kind of review it, to be able to kind of understand the kind of effects of how the law might change, and what the nuances are, right?

st.t: Delivery economics: AI pressures pricing and apprenticeship
st.an: The interview supports the cluster’s core account: growing in-house adoption can pressure outside counsel, shared AI workspaces can reshape firm–client delivery, and lawyers may shift from document-level production toward reviewing outputs and managing work. Its claims are qualitative and predictive rather than measured, consistent with the cluster’s caution that market-wide transformation and productivity effects remain unproven.
qs: We've seen growing within the corporate legal side, more and more teams are starting to adopt AI, and then it becomes an expectation that your outside council is also utilizing AI.
You go from being the technical worker to more the kind of the manager.

st.t: Harvey strategy: Prestige supports infrastructure ambitions
st.an: The source is consistent with the synthesis’s qualified view: legal AI can support productised client services, while Harvey’s prestige and adoption do not by themselves establish superior product differentiation. Its reported preference for Legora is anecdotal and unmeasured, reinforcing rather than resolving the cluster’s defensibility dispute.
qs: It's almost like you want to say like a freebie that they give to their clients to show that they are partners and not that, hey, we're just charging you for everything that we do.
And he told me they had seen Harvey, they weren't impressed, they had moved on.

st.t: In-house adoption: Stronger buyers may insource selectively
st.an: The source supports the proposition that growing in-house AI adoption strengthens corporate legal teams and can shift routine work internally, while rejecting a universal outside-counsel decline. It emphasises collaborative, configurable workspaces through which firms can guide clients and remain involved, aligning with selective insourcing and a non-zero-sum provider relationship.
qs: We've seen growing within the corporate legal side, more and more teams are starting to adopt AI, and then it becomes an expectation that your outside council is also utilizing AI.

You know, when you receive an NDA, we want to just quickly be able to flag, what are the risks, what's low, what's high risk, and then get the tool to use our knowledge to start providing our suggestions of how we can bring this in line with our policies.

st.t: Legal software: Workflow layers defend specialist value
st.an: Legora supports the cluster’s core proposition that specialist value lies in a legal workflow layer built around general large language models, here through a multi-step agent rather than fine-tuning. It also aligns with the copilot framing by preserving lawyers’ last-mile involvement and ownership, although its speed and accuracy claims are promotional and lack independent evaluation.
qs: Rather, we've built an agent that has different steps, a different process that it goes through to articulate the questions that has been given, and then to kind of apply that to legal thinking, as opposed to trying to fine tune the models to have ChatGPT that understands law.
Lawyers want that, meaning a lawyer wants to have, I want to be able to do some of the last mile bit of this, that I still feel like value and I still feel some ownership over the product.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s principal proposition: AI is expected to automate document-intensive production and shift lawyers toward review, judgment, management and client-facing work rather than eliminate their continuing role. It also aligns with bounded copilot use, active human verification, selective contraction of the junior layer and buyer-side pressure, while relying mainly on promotional observations and anecdotes rather than independent evidence.
qs: You go from being the technical worker to more the kind of the manager.
And frankly, the quality of AI is not really at the point where you're going to just trust an agent to go and do that work for you and just blindly send it to a client, right?

st.t: Vendor value: Concentration forecasts face diverse competition
st.an: Williams supports the cluster’s account that specialist vendors may seek value through ecosystem partnerships and user-community learning beyond model access. His remarks describe Legora’s intended strategy, but provide no measured evidence that it creates durable differentiation, performance gains or returns.
qs: And how do we make sure that we are collaborating with the right players in the market, whether that be from implementation or publishers, to make sure that we can get Legora to the people who want to use it.
They can come and share ideas and share what they've learned, share their failures, share their successes, and get a bit of a voice to help drive the change forward.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Legora supports the cluster’s core proposition that legal AI should be deployed selectively within collaborative, human-led workflows. It presents AI as useful for task-specific document work while rejecting unsupervised client delivery, retaining lawyer review, control and accountability, and predicting role redesign rather than wholesale lawyer replacement. Its productivity and staffing claims are primarily first-party observations and forecasts, not independent evidence.
qs: And frankly, the quality of AI is not really at the point where you're going to just trust an agent to go and do that work for you and just blindly send it to a client, right?
It's a key shift, because I think that the chat interface is not going away anytime soon, but there's a lot of other ways that we can utilize AI for different tasks in a much more effective way.

kp.k: Generative AI shifts sales toward client-led discovery
kp.d: Williams contrasts his experience selling no-code/low-code products, which required extensive discovery and persuasion, with selling Legora: demonstrations prompt lawyers to identify applications themselves. He argues that the earlier premise that anyone could build applications did not fit lawyers' willingness to do so. This is a vendor's experiential account, not a measured adoption comparison.
qs: And lawyers are not going to go building their own applications.

So it's like also, it's very much like, as you say, that kind of client-led discovery because they also, they now want to explore how this technology can support them, as opposed to, as you said previously, like having to find a pain point that you could anchor a sale on.

kp.k: Rebranding expresses a collaborative legal-AI strategy
kp.d: Williams presents the change from Leya to Legora as reflecting rapid company and platform maturation and an ambition to connect lawyers, clients and AI. Collaboration also means combining lawyers' domain expertise with the vendor's technical expertise as capabilities develop. He expects legal practice to change over five or ten years while emphasizing uncertainty about AI's position even one year ahead.
qs: And our goal is really to build the world's first truly collaborative AI for lawyers.
So how do we make sure that we bring in lawyers, their clients and machines together in an effective way to deliver value?
No one can truly say in one year this is where AI is going to be.
You bring the domain expertise, we bring the technical expertise, and we collaborate.

kp.k: Task-specific interfaces complement chat and enable shared work
kp.d: Williams describes shared AI workspaces and tabular document review as alternatives to solitary chat interactions. He claims users can extract information across thousands of documents in tables, then use chat to interpret results or draft risk reports. His document-volume and speed statements describe vendor-claimed capabilities rather than independently tested performance.
qs: How do we open it up so that a team can actually work with AI in one singular environment?
You can start to really analyze and extract all the key information across thousands of documents.
You could then take that result into a chat interface and say, well, now that I've analyzed this, I need to start interpreting it, I need to write a report of the risks.
I mean, as I say, you can literally take 10,000 documents, throw them into a table, go grab yourself a cup of coffee and you've got all of your information there.

kp.k: In-house adoption changes expectations of outside counsel
kp.d: Williams reports growing corporate legal adoption, driven partly by resource constraints and difficulty funding additional staff. He says this creates expectations that outside counsel also use AI and motivates shared client-firm workspaces. Rather than primarily describing clients adopting because firms fail to act, he reports firms proactively helping clients adopt the technology.
qs: We've seen growing within the corporate legal side, more and more teams are starting to adopt AI, and then it becomes an expectation that your outside council is also utilizing AI.
It can become very difficult to get budget to bring in additional hands.
So they become that kind of strategic lead for a lot of their clients in the adoption of AI.

kp.k: Configurable playbooks address different buyer and provider workflows
kp.d: Williams stresses that in-house departments and law firms operate differently. He describes configurable foundational tools, including a Word add-in with playbooks that flag NDA risks and suggest changes aligned with organizational policies. He presents this as useful both for time-constrained in-house teams and for firms performing some NDA reviews without billing to sustain client relationships.
qs: The way that an in-house team operates and the way that a law firm operates are fundamentally different.
So you can now build playbooks into the word add-in, which becomes super powerful for in-house teams.

You know, when you receive an NDA, we want to just quickly be able to flag, what are the risks, what's low, what's high risk, and then get the tool to use our knowledge to start providing our suggestions of how we can bring this in line with our policies.
And equally, if you look at the law firms, in a lot of cases, that is work that they will do for their clients without billing for it.

kp.k: Legora emphasizes agent workflows rather than model fine-tuning
kp.d: Asked about Harvey, Williams acknowledges common underlying large language model technology and similar features, but describes different implementation approaches. He says Legora had not fine-tuned models, instead building an agent with steps for interpreting questions and applying legal thinking. He emphasizes flexible core tools rather than customer-specific software. These are vendor descriptions, not comparative evaluation findings.
qs: There's a lot of features that are very similar to one another.
Yeah, and we've also, we took fundamentally different approaches at the start, where we haven't done any fine tuning of the models.

Rather, we've built an agent that has different steps, a different process that it goes through to articulate the questions that has been given, and then to kind of apply that to legal thinking, as opposed to trying to fine tune the models to have ChatGPT that understands law.

kp.k: Rapid development is presented as a competitive differentiator
kp.d: Williams reports new products or features every two weeks and a Word playbook feature built in just over a week. He predicts that development speed can allow Legora to overtake competitors during a one-year software contract and make competing tools unused. The asserted competitive trajectory is a sales-oriented prediction, not a documented longitudinal comparison.
qs: Like I've seen every two weeks, there's just been like new product, new features being released to the platform.
We decided to build like a playbook feature within the Word add-in and that was built in just over a week.

Even if we are slightly behind at the start of the year, you know for a fact that if you buy Legora, by a couple of months in, it surpasses the other tool and the other tools is going to become shelf-ware because your lawyers and you won't obviously use the best tech.

kp.k: AI changes software-building economics and legal-market attractiveness
kp.d: Williams contrasts six months of training for basic no-code/low-code application building with his anecdote of creating a product-feedback portal through a few prompts in five minutes. He argues that legal's high cost per task and newly capable underlying models attract stronger entrepreneurial talent. His account of Legora's origins identifies ChatGPT 3.5 as making an earlier document-review idea practically valuable; these are experience-based claims rather than systematic investment evidence.
qs: You have to train someone for six months to get them up to speed, to then build an app that was, they could do things, but it was still very basic in terms of the applications you were building.
That was a couple of prompts and five minutes later I had an application.
But what you see is the cost per task in legal is way higher than in most other industries.
And then as soon as ChatGPT 3.5 came out, the technology was suddenly in a place where it could actually be very valuable towards legal work.

kp.k: Agents plan and execute multi-step work
kp.d: Williams distinguishes agents from direct query-and-output chat by their decomposition of a query into steps, planning and execution, or execution of a supplied workflow. He expects this process to improve output quality. Abramowitz's stronger framing of agents as an order-of-magnitude change is the host's proposition; Williams offers a functional explanation without measured performance evidence.
qs: Whereas if you look at it from an agent perspective is, here's my query, understand the query, break it down, what are different steps that need to be taken in order to achieve this, and then making a plan to then go and execute that using their knowledge, execute the plan and then come back saying, well, now here's the output, which is just going to give you a much higher level of quality.
And then that agent can go work through those different steps.

kp.k: Human verification remains necessary for accountable legal work
kp.d: Williams rejects blindly sending autonomous-agent work to clients at current quality levels. He calls for lawyers to retain control, review outputs and iterate. He connects this human involvement to the firm's professional assurance and insurance-backed risk mitigation for clients, rather than presenting AI as a replacement for accountable legal service delivery.
qs: And frankly, the quality of AI is not really at the point where you're going to just trust an agent to go and do that work for you and just blindly send it to a client, right?
You want to be able to review the work is doing.
So you don't want to just put your stamp of like, this is our work without actually being in the loop and being in the one that's in control of that.

kp.k: Automation reallocates time toward billable and relationship work
kp.d: Williams presents several possible uses of efficiency gains: improved work-life balance, less non-billable work, and more time understanding clients and developing business. He specifically argues that technical legal excellence alone does not assure partnership, drawing on another podcast, and identifies cross-selling between litigation and real estate as a concrete use of freed time. These are proposed mechanisms and examples, not measured revenue or billing outcomes.
qs: whether that's to make sure you can finish your work before midnight or you can spend some time with your family
A core reason why a lot of partners become partners is because they're really strategic business developers.

And that allows you to develop deeper relationships with them, to find different business that you can also do for them, and then be able to become really strategic in helping to develop the business for your firm, right?
At the end of the day, going through mounds of paperwork is not as valuable as making sure that now this client that uses you for litigation now also uses you for real estate.

kp.k: Junior-heavy work shifts toward experienced oversight
kp.d: Williams describes lawyers moving from document-processing work toward managing and reviewing AI output. Referring to an unspecified pie chart, he says the junior share is shrinking while the mid-senior share grows, requiring earlier progression into judgment-intensive roles. No underlying dataset, period or staffing ratio is supplied. He emphasizes management, critical thinking and business-development skills rather than merely faster technical production.
qs: You go from being the technical worker to more the kind of the manager.
It's like you're not necessarily having to write the exam, you more have to mark the exam.
And if you look at them all at equal portions, you see that that kind of real junior layer is shrinking. And the kind of mid-senior lawyers, that part of the chart is growing.

You have to become a lot more kind of strategic, a lot more critical in your thinking, and develop a lot more kind of management skills, business development skills, so that you can just utilize your time in a more effective way.

kp.k: Complex contracts still require deep legal expertise
kp.d: Williams reports an example involving a highly complex contract with multiple dependencies and nuances, which he says AI can struggle to handle. He uses getting '50%' of the way there as an illustration of partial assistance, with lawyers' domain knowledge needed to complete the work; this is not presented as a benchmarked completion rate.
qs: we had a someone that was trying to review a highly complex contract, with multiple dependencies, lots of kind of nuances in it.
AI as a whole can really struggle with that.
So being able to take that deep legal expertise that they have, get AI to get you 50% of the way there, and then to use your domain knowledge to really execute the work.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Chris Williams claims generative AI changes legal-technology purchasing from salesperson-led problem discovery to lawyer-led exploration of readily visible capabilities.
pts.d: Drawing on his transition from selling no-code/low-code products to Legora, Williams says lawyers struggled to envisage building applications themselves, whereas AI demonstrations prompt them to identify relevant uses. He describes litigation chronologies appearing almost immediately and large-scale document review taking seconds. These are accounts of demonstrations and sales experience, rather than reported performance tests.

pts.k: Williams presents shared, task-specific AI workspaces as a shift from individual chatbot use toward collaboration among lawyers, clients and AI.
pts.d: He describes current matter-level collaboration features and tabular review for extracting information across thousands of documents, followed by chat-based interpretation or risk reporting. Bringing lawyers and clients into one AI workspace is also an expressed product ambition. He does not predict the disappearance of chat; different interfaces are intended to support different tasks.

pts.k: Williams says in-house AI adoption both addresses constrained resources and creates expectations that outside counsel will use AI.
pts.d: He reports growing corporate legal adoption, motivated partly by difficulty securing additional headcount and the desire to free time for strategic work. He also says some law firms proactively guide clients' AI adoption rather than waiting for client demands. Word-based playbooks illustrate how common technology can serve different workflows: in-house teams can flag NDA risks and suggest policy-aligned changes, while firms can reduce the effort associated with NDA reviews they sometimes provide without billing.

pts.k: Williams claims agent-based processing improves legal AI output, but says current quality requires lawyer control and verification rather than autonomous client delivery.
pts.d: He says Legora uses an agent that breaks questions into steps and applies legal concepts, rather than fine-tuning its underlying models. He argues planning and execution produce higher-quality answers than immediate chat responses. This is a claimed mechanism, without comparative results. His model is augmentation: lawyers must review and potentially iterate on outputs before adopting them as the firm's work, particularly because clients rely on the firm's responsibility and insurance.

pts.k: Williams predicts lawyers will shift from document-heavy execution toward reviewing AI work, exercising judgment, managing work and developing client business.
pts.d: He argues that reducing mundane and non-billable work can free lawyers to understand clients, deepen relationships and identify additional instructions, such as winning real-estate work from a litigation client. He also identifies efficiency and personal time as possible benefits, rather than assuming every saved hour becomes additional revenue. For highly complex contracts, he explicitly retains a major role for expert legal judgment.

pts.k: Williams describes a shrinking junior share and growing mid-senior share of legal staffing, with lawyers expected to take on review responsibilities earlier.
pts.d: He invokes an unspecified pie chart to describe this shift, linking it to AI taking over mundane heavy lifting. The transcript supplies no chart source, workforce dataset, quantified change or implementation date. His statement concerns relative role composition and earlier progression into judgment-intensive work; it does not establish an absolute headcount reduction or provide a forecast for partner numbers.

pts.k: Williams claims generative AI has made legal technology more attractive to entrepreneurs and enabled rapid product development that can displace competing software.
pts.d: He attributes the change to high legal cost per task and the capabilities available after ChatGPT 3.5. He describes an AI-built application of his own taking five minutes, Legora releasing features roughly every two weeks, and a Word playbook feature built in just over a week. He predicts that even if Legora initially trails another product, its development speed will let it overtake that product within months of a one-year contract, potentially leaving the competitor unused. These are vendor experience and competitive predictions, not independent comparative findings.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence offered is predominantly Williams's vendor-side experience, product descriptions and illustrative customer anecdotes.
pts.d: Williams is Legora's head of strategic partnerships and community. He supports claims through sales encounters, product demonstrations, development examples and an unnamed complex-contract user's experience. The staffing claim references an unidentified chart. No independently documented benchmarks, accuracy rates, controlled productivity studies, client outcome measurements or workforce datasets are supplied. The host's second-hand comparison of Harvey and Legora is not treated as evidence of demonstrated superiority. Numerical descriptions of document speed and AI completing 50% of complex work remain Williams's illustrative claims.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The interview combines present-tense adoption and capability claims with an uncertain five-to-ten-year transformation outlook.
pts.d: The conversation was recorded in late February for release in March 2025. Williams describes collaboration, tabular review and Word playbooks as existing capabilities, and staffing and role changes as underway or emerging without a firm deadline. He expects legal work to look different in five or ten years but explicitly rejects confidence about AI's position even one year ahead. Current autonomy is qualified by output quality, human review and complex-contract limitations. His competitive displacement forecast is much shorter: a few months within a typical one-year software contract.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The claimed effects concern law-firm lawyers, in-house teams, corporate clients and legal-software suppliers.
pts.d: Litigators and document reviewers gain faster information extraction; juniors face earlier demands for review and judgment; experienced lawyers retain responsibility for complex analysis and verification. Firms may reduce non-billable effort and expand client relationships. Resource-constrained in-house departments may gain capacity and influence outside counsel's AI use. Corporate clients may collaborate more directly with firms while continuing to rely on firm accountability. Software suppliers face faster competition, while Legora reports hiring across commercial, legal-engineering and software-engineering roles. The source makes no concrete access-to-justice claim or prediction of profession-wide lawyer elimination.
